text:
Part 2, The Falcon, Then the Road

Calden did not let the talk become philosophy. Philosophy was how a hall missed a boy. “His name is Orlog Stone. Eleven. Loft-shine noticed, packet consented, Vaelund a month. Teaching and care. Those terms travel or I will hear it from a kitchen that already paid.”
“Jorunn,” the older man said, surprising no one who had ever kept western accounts, and surprising Harland, who had not expected the forest to know a high-farm name. “She will climb if you make a thief of the promise.”
“Then do not.”
“And the brother.” Not a question.
“On my roof tonight. On my green at first bell. I am not sending you the whole house.”
“Good. I have shelves. I do not have a garrison.” The silk moved when he breathed. “You understand what you are asking. A state school is a Power’s tool. I am not a Power. I am a man who keeps doors. If I take him, your falcon becomes a policy whether you put it on Harland’s book or not.”
“Then it is a policy.” Calden’s voice stayed level. Urgency had already been spent on the bird. “Worthy of you, or not safe enough where he is, or both. I am done choosing the pretty word. Take him.”
The older man touched two fingers to the air where the wall had been. The dark did not open yet. It considered. Destinations desired by an owner did not run on lordly feeling; they ran on the owner’s will, and the will was being asked to point at a mill-race inland and a boy with a slate.
“I will look,” he said. “If the Cut has made a prison of a school I will take him because you asked and because I do not like prisons that use broth as an alibi. If it has made a school of a school I will take him anyway, because you have never once sent that bird for a trifle, and I am too old to pretend tonight is the first time.”
Paella said, “Teaching and care. Say it back so a holding can hear it.”
The older man looked faintly amused, which on that mouth was almost respect. “Teaching and care. I keep both, or you may send the next bird with a stone tied to it.”
No one laughed. It had not been a joke large enough for laughter. It had been an account.
“Stay in this room,” he said, not unkindly, to Harland. “If you follow, you will write what you see, and I do not require a folio of my threshold.”
Harland stayed.
The wall remembered how to be elsewhere. Silk, mute as bark, stepped into it. The tallow-flame leaned, recovered, and went on selling the hour it had been paid for.
The question that had been for the ears of the room only settled into the beams the way smoke does: present, and not repeatable on the green.
The Compact That Has to Travel
They did not speak immediately after the dark became a wall again. A hall that has just been used as a landing wants a moment to admit it is still a hall.
Harland found ink because ink was how he stopped a miracle from becoming a rumor. He wrote, in the off-book hand: Bird answered. Man received. Terms restated. Teaching. Care. Boy to be moved from Vaelund-on-the-Cut. Reason: duty. He did not write the question. He did not write the name. He did not write both.
“If Vaelund refuses,” he said, “the Power will ask why a coastal hold with a new mast thinks it can edit a state folio.”
“Then the Power may ask,” Calden said. “I keep their road. I keep their magazine. I keep their ridge from being only a needle. They may have a question. I have a child who was called a convenience on my grass.”
Paella set the cup down. “You should send word to the Stones before the forest does it by absence. Jorunn consented to a school. She did not consent to a vanishing.”
“In the morning. A night packet is a panic. I will not pay for panic twice.”
“Morning, then. Not a rumor in the fish market.”
“Harland will walk it. Not a sergeant. Not a magazine-mouth.”
Harland’s mouth twitched. “I would have walked it without being forbidden the other options.”
“I know.”
Paella thought in a different column. Aimed light. Read light. Light put out on command. The Cut taught starting and stopping because a Power that could only ignite was a Power that would someday set its own holdings on fire. The forest would teach spending: when a page becomes a weapon, when a weapon becomes a shrine, when a shrine becomes a policy. She would have the three who stayed. She would not awaken a western mark in a boy to make her husband’s urgency feel blessed. Marks woke when the work was ready. Work was not ready on a Sólardag night because a falcon had been brave.
“The three will see the empty place,” she said. “Not tonight. Soon. Voss will think the packet has happened twice.”
“Then I will tell Voss the compact moved. Not the joke. Not the bird. The compact.” Calden rubbed his thumb against the slate’s edge. “He used Lord today. He can hear a sentence that does not soothe him.”
“And Holme?”
“Holme is a schoolmaster who writes what he is told to write. I do not need him to be a villain. I need him to yield a folio without pretending the folio is the child.”
That was the whole of the traveling compact: the boy was not the writing. The care could not stay behind like a chair. If the forest forgot any part of that, Jorunn would climb.
“Go to bed,” Paella said to both of them, which in her mouth was not softness. “If you stand here until he returns with a child, you will make the return into a theatre. The green already had one of those today.”
Calden went as far as the stair. He did not sleep. He stood in the dark of his own passage and practiced the pace he would need at first bell, when Rigg would put wood back into the hands of children who did not yet know that precision and damage were a single trade, and that the lord who tested them had already spent the night moving their friend’s brother off a map they could walk.
The Cut, Which Had Not Failed Yet
Orlog Stone was awake because fourth-bell thinking did not respect inland hours.
Vaelund-on-the-Cut smelled of wet stone, mill-grain, and the particular ink that state schools bought by the pot. The wheel on the near bank took what the inland holdings were bound to bring. Suit of mill. He had watched it the way he had once watched a Wick dip: a thing with a temper, a thing that charged even when it was still.
He had written Voss an inventory because an inventory could travel without becoming a warrant for climbing. Bed. Broth. Hour held. Letters arrived. He had not written the passage argument about metering new lights like mill-rights versus refusing an invented dark age. That argument was seed, not a letter.
Holme’s care was not love. It was broth, bread, coat, bells, path-privilege when the folio was clean. Orlog, who withheld emote so Jorunn would not treat a feeling as a reason to reclaim him, found that arrangement usable. If the teaching failed he would say so. It had not failed. He could start a shine on command. He could stop one, which was harder. A loft-night taught survival of a page. A hall taught the page that dusk was also a tool.
He did not make a light.
He was eleven. He was not short. He was written.
When the wall of the side passage — a wall he had walked past sixteen times in a week and counted, because counting was how he kept from being only a feeling — remembered a forest, Orlog did not reach for a shine. He reached for the slate. A slate is a tool. A shine is a spending.
Holme was in the passage faster than a man looks in a night-shirt. He saw the dark that was not Vaelund dark. He saw the mute silk. He did not say a name. He said, “This pupil is under compact.”
“I know the compact,” the older man said. “I am here to keep it in a different house. You may yield the folio or you may make a theatre. I have seen a theatre today already, at one remove, and I am not collecting a second.”
Orlog stood. The issued coat made him look like no one’s son, which was the point of it. He looked at the beard, the cloth, the draft that smelled faintly of paper that had never known fish. He did not look for Voss. Voss was a post he had told to stay standing.
Holme’s jaw worked once. “Stone. You will take your pouch and your slate. You will not take the house-coat. The house-coat stays on the Cut.”
That was not cruelty. That was inventory. Orlog fetched the applewood-pricked pouch Jorunn had given him the night before the packet — teeth, house-runes, western grandmother’s remembering — and the slate, and the two letters he was allowed to keep. He left the coat on the peg. He put on the plain thing Calder had sent because a father would not have a son walk into anyone’s elsewhere looking issued.
“Are you a school,” Orlog asked the older man, because the question was the compact and because he would not climb for Jorunn if he could still ask it.
“I am a library that has not forgotten how to teach. You will be fed. You will be taught. You will be written only as much as a page requires, not as much as a Power enjoys. If that fails, you will say so in a letter your mother can carry up a stair. I would prefer you never have to write it.”
Holme heard the care-floor restated and chose, in the small courage available to men who keep other people’s children, not to make a shrine of his mill-race. “The folio will note transfer under surety of Austervik’s hall. I will not note a kidnapping.”
“Good,” the older man said. “Kidnapping is a word for men who do not keep accounts.”
Orlog looked once at the wheel in the dark. He had not hated it. He had not been meant to stay long enough to hate it. A month was a school. A month was also a waiting room if a falcon had already decided the next room.
He stepped when he was told to step. The slate was under his arm. The pouch was against his ribs. The shine stayed unspent. Aimed light, loft-light, star-count, sculpted fire, door-light — Entrares had more words for spending than any one boy was allowed to use in a night. He used none of them.
The passage ceased to be Vaelund.
Destinations Their Owner Desires
There was a step that was not a step.
Orlog’s stomach offered an opinion and was ignored. When the dark agreed to be a room, it was a room that went up.
Five stories of library do not announce themselves to an eleven-year-old as five. They announce themselves as a throat. Shelves rose until looking became a kind of kneeling. Ladders ran on rails that had been waxed by a hand that respected both wood and time. Here and there a door sat in the stacks the way a dip sits in a row of dips: ordinary, until you understood it was not. Some of those doors would open onto pocket-weather — rooms that did not share foundations, workbenches where evocation had been told to happen inside a box so the box, and not the forest, would take the scorch. Contained fire. Sculpted force. Light that could be aimed until it became a profession. Orlog felt all of that the way he had felt Maera’s kettle: as temper, as craft, as a thing that would punish a boy who treated it like a toy.
Other doors would not open for his wanting. He could desire Austervik until his teeth hurt. He could desire Voss. He could desire the Wick yard and a copper box and a four-hour dip that had been honest. The door would keep its owner. Ownership was the lock. One day, if he served, he might be taught to knock. Knocking was not owning.
“You may speak,” the older man said. “You may also be silent. I do not grade the first night.”
Orlog set the slate on the nearest table that did not look like a trick. “Is this Castaras.”
“It is in Castaras. It does not use the Cut. Those are different facts.”
“Does my brother know.”
“He will know a compact moved. He will not know this room until someone who owns a door decides he may. I am not in the business of fetching garrisons into my stacks.”
Orlog nodded once. Inventory. He could live in inventory. The pouch under his coat had the small, unmagical weight of teeth and house-runes. Blessing of Bones was not chapel-work and not this tower’s work. It was Jorunn’s remembering. He intended to keep the columns separate. Mixed columns were how a boy became a shrine.
“You will eat. Then you will sleep in a bed that is not issued. In the morning we will find out whether you can stop a light as well as you start one. I am told you can. I prefer to see it. Starting is a loft. Stopping is a life.”
“Holme already saw it.”
“Holme is a school. I am a trade.” The correction was not unkind. “Evocation is not a miracle and it is not a tantrum. It is a way of telling force where to stand. If you serve here you will learn to spend a page so that the page does work and does not become a religion. Your brother’s green has already tried to make you a religion once today, at a distance. I will not repeat the experiment.”
Orlog’s mouth did the thing it did when he almost felt and chose a count instead. “Voss ended someone.”
“So I gathered, from a bird that does not usually carry theater.” A pause. “Did he end him enough, or too much.”
“I wasn’t there.”
“You will be, in the only way that matters. He will keep ending things until someone teaches him the difference between a finish and a court. That will not be my office. I keep you. The green keeps him. If the two offices ever share a hull, that will be a later account.”
Orlog did not hear the later account. He heard bed, broth, hour, door. He was eleven. He was enough.
He ate what was put in front of him. It was better than Vaelund and he did not put that on a letter. He slept in a bed that smelled of cedar and not of mill-wet. Once, near whatever inland hour corresponded to a coastal first bell, he felt — not a shine, not a mark, a draft — as if a shield-cut on a forearm he was not touching had flexed in its sleep. He did not write that down either.
Below the tower the forest kept its own banalité: dark, and the right to remain dark, and no Power collecting fee-farm from the owls. Magick, here, was not municipal. It was a throat of books and a man who could afford silk the color of bark. Means and Magick in one spine. Orlog turned his face into the cedar and practiced being a person after being moved, which was the work Holme had not had time to assign.
First Bell, Which Did Not Know the Forest
Austervik’s first bell did what first bells do. It did not ask the hall whether a child had changed rooms in the night.
Rigg was on the green before the three were. Sergeant. Colm when the hall books needed two words. Rigg when the rail needed one. Dueling man. Shield on the arm that was not the lesson-arm. He did not take the other rack. The other rack was for boys being measured as finishers. He was the measuring.
“Stone. Cordia. Wick.” He did not say good morning. Morning was not a favor. “The lord tested you yesterday in public. That is not a method I can use every Sólardag or the green becomes a chapel. Today I teach. If you make a court of my teaching I will put you back on the timber until your feet learn the difference.”
Pallis took the heavier wood as if he had been waiting his whole life to be told it was allowed. Brinean took the blade she was allowed and looked, once, at the butts. Rigg’s chin did not tip her away. The allowance had not been unmade. Bow first was still the office. Being in the row was the measuring.
Voss put both hands on the waster and left the post standing when he hit it. Calden’s price and Orlog’s price, still briefly in agreement.
They worked.
Rigg taught the thing Calden would test later without naming either word as a thesis: place the strike; make the placed strike carry enough to end what it started. Precision without damage was a pretty miss. Damage without precision was Bram Harth’s mouth and a habit of courts. He demonstrated once, Dueling-clean, shield employed as a second decision, not as a hiding place.
“Again,” Rigg said, which was the whole curriculum.
Paella came at the second hour, not onto the grass, to the hall end of the rail. Court first: how to stand in a room that was deciding something. Letters second: Voss slower than the post, Pallis impatient with a nib, Brinean unexpectedly exact, as if a mold-hand already knew that a line either held or it did not.
Ability third, and only the look of it.
She did not call a shine. She did not touch Voss’s sleeve. She set a wick in a dish — Wick-work, bought, honest — and asked them what family the flame belonged to. Purchased. Rationed. Not a miracle. Then she asked them what family an unbought loft-light belonged to, and what family a star-count belonged to, and whether those families were allowed to marry.
Brinean said, “A star-count is aimed.”
Paella’s mouth allowed that. “Aimed is the beginning of court. A loft-shine wants a page to live. An aimed light wants a thing to be seen, or to fall, or both. If you ever spend one, you will know which you meant. If you do not know, you will not spend it on my floor.”
Voss kept his sleeve down. The coal under the skin wanted, for the first time since Hallva, to be asked a question by someone who knew how to ask it without making a shrine. Paella did not ask.
Calden came at the third hour and tested once. One pass. One fail that was not a humiliation. No speech. He looked at Voss the way a man looks at a post he has decided not to spend.
“Your brother is under the same compact in a different house,” he said, only to Voss, and only after the fail had been corrected. “Teaching and care. You will not make a second packet of it on my grass. You will not climb. If climbing is required, a house that is allowed to climb will do it.”
Voss said, “Yes, Lord.”
He did not ask where. He understood, without liking it, that not-knowing was part of the compact now.
Rigg put the wood back into his hands. “Again.”
Far from the channel, in a throat of books, an eleven-year-old stopped a shine on command for a man in mute silk and was told, “Pass. Again. Different glass.” The two rooms did not share a foundation. They shared a floor that had been made to travel. That would have to be enough for a Sólardag’s aftermath.
The Second Half, Which Had Been Mercy
Bram Harth had been off the magazine timber for one night and already hated the shape of air that did not include a watch.
Ten days was the first half. He had said the required sentence in the row with a ruined lip and the words had not improved the lip. Noll Reeve’s wrist was wrapped in the kind of cloth a man uses when he does not want a healer to ask him a question. They stood in the lee of the timber stack on the lane-side of the magazine, where the holding’s eye had to turn a corner to finish its work, and they watched Voss Stone come off the green at the pause between Rigg’s again and Paella’s hour.
He was alone because Pallis had been kept at the rail to correct a dip and Brinean had been sent to the butts with a single look that meant the allowance still existed. The lane was a lane. Bram had been a magazine-man yesterday. He still thought like one: concentrated stores, concentrated loot, concentrated boys.
“Not steel,” Noll said, which was the whole of his wisdom and the reason the thing that followed could be called nothing too serious by anyone who had not been inside it.
“Not steel,” Bram agreed. His mouth hurt when he agreed.
They stepped out together because together was the point. Yesterday the three had been a court. Today they would prove the one in the middle was only a quay carpenter’s height without his shadows.
Voss saw them late. Alert was Rigg’s feat, not his. He had time to think, with the stupid clarity of a person who has been told not to make a habit of courts, that this was a court anyway, and that Calden’s grass was not present to price it.
Bram hit first, shoulder and fist, the magazine weight of a young man who was not thirteen. Voss went into the stack hard enough to taste bark. The mark on his forearm flared heat — not light, never light, a buried coal kicking — and for a breath that wanted to be a future he could have spent it. A shield-cut answering a blow the way Hallva had said he would be used. He did not spend it. Orlog’s page had been clear. A strike without a target spends, and then someone has to name it. Bram Harth was a target. The mark was not a tool he had been given permission to use on a lane.
He used his hands.
Noll came from the other side, clumsy with the wrapped wrist, precise enough with the free one. A scrape opened on Voss’s cheek. A bruise found the ribs Calder had been teaching him to keep over. He got an elbow into Bram’s already-ruined mouth and felt the mercy of yesterday crack. Pallis was not there to take a knee. Brinean was not there with a stave. The geometry was two and one, and the one was the boy who had ended it too cleanly in public.
Precision, Rigg had said, without using the word as a sermon. Place it. Make the placed thing enough.
Voss stopped swinging as if the stack were a shrine. He took the next fist on his shoulder instead of his head, stepped the way Calder kicked a foot on the strand, and put his weight into a single short blow that had a location. Bram’s wind went. The magazine-man sat down without deciding to. Noll tried to make the two-on-one true again and met the waster-callus of a hand that had been on heavier wood since first bell. Not a finish that wrecked. A finish that ended. Noll joined Bram on the lane-dirt with his good wrist singing and his wrapped one held like a secret.
Voss stood. Scraped. Bruised. Breathing like a person who had almost opened a door in his own skin and had left it shut. Blood on his cheek no worse than a quay-day. The coal under the sleeve settled, disappointed or pleased — he had no office that could tell those apart yet.
He did not kick them. Kicking was a court.
Rigg arrived at a run that still had room to be a charge if a charge had been required. He took in the stack, the two on the dirt, the one still standing, the absence of steel.
“Up,” he said to Harth and Reeve, and the word had Dueling in it, which was to say it did not need a second word.
Calden came because Rigg sent a boy who was not Voss, and because a lord who has spent a night moving a compact does not get to miss the second half of a sentence he himself delayed.
He looked at Voss first. Scrapes, bruising, the sleeve still down, the post of the boy still standing. “Did you end it.”
“Yes, Lord.”
“Did you wreck them.”
“No, Lord.”
“Then you may keep the heavier wood.” Calden turned to Bram and Noll as if they were a slate. “Yesterday I priced a mouth. I left a road attached to a warning because I am not in the habit of unmaking a magazine for one sentence. You have now used hands where I told you not to make a court. That is the second half.”
Bram’s eyes did the math of a man who has just watched mercy close.
“Harth. You will not stand my timber. You will not take my road. There is work enough in this town for a back that cannot keep a watch. If I find you on my magazine lane again I will find you a road that is not Castaras. Reeve. You seconded a joke and then you seconded a beating. You will go with him. I do not keep a pair.”
Noll started a word and swallowed it. The wrist had already spoken.
“Stone. You will have those cleaned at Kell’s water and be on the rail after. You will not collect a shrine from a lane. Wick and Cordia will not be told this was glory. It was a double that failed. That is the whole tale.”
Voss said yes. He tasted bark and blood and the particular metal of a mark that had agreed, for one more day, to remain a shield.
Rigg took him by the nape as a sergeant does, which is not a hug and is not an arrest, and steered him toward water. Behind them Bram Harth looked at the magazine he would not climb again and found that a holding’s mercy had always had a second half. It had only been waiting for a lane.
The green, when Voss returned to it, was still a green. First bell had already been spent. Again was still the curriculum. Precision. Enough. Not a court. Not a shrine. The road that left with Harth and Reeve was the sentence the grass had promised and then, for one night, withheld.
Voss put his hands on the wood. He left the post standing. The coal under his sleeve kept its lid. The story that would someday teach him to take the lid off without becoming a religion had not arrived. The story that had: a falcon. A letter with one name. A door that was not a hall door. A brother moved. A double that failed. A mercy completed.
He hit the post where Rigg pointed, and the pointing, for the first time, felt like a target that was allowed to be a target.

text:
A flower blooming in the far north—a single blossom pushing through soil that was once solid ice—is a powerful metaphor. It reframes a warming world not as an ending, but as an awakening of unwritten potential.

The retreat of permafrost brings this vision into focus. Millions of square kilometres of frozen ground could gradually open to human enterprise, echoing how Norse settlers established agriculture along the coastal fjords of Greenland during the Medieval Warm Period.

High latitudes have long been defined by stillness—vast, locked expanses of ice, tundra, and boreal shadow. Yet beneath that quiet frost lies a new frontier. As the climate envelope shifts, it brings an unprecedented geographic realignment, exposing vast northern reaches to extended summer sun.

To look across those northern horizons of Canada, Russia, and the high latitudes only to see mud and engineering friction is to misread human history. Every frontier humanity has conquered—from the low countries of Europe to the tallgrass prairies of North America—was initially written off as an unlivable swamp or barren plain.

History does not belong to the faint-hearted; it belongs to the builders, innovators, and farmers who look at dynamic terrain and see the foundation for a new era.

The shift will demand extraordinary ingenuity. Building on unstable ground, developing short-season crops tuned to long daylight hours, and nurturing acidic tundra into fertile loam will require patience, capital, and engineering.

Yet the potential dividend is vast: expanded agricultural capacity, vital maritime trade corridors and new settlements. In an era often dominated by anxiety, the northern expansion offers a practical vision of adaptation and growth.

A flower blooming in ground that was once frozen permafrost is more than an ecological shift—a symbol of human ingenuity finding a way.

text:
Washington State 

August 30, 2026

I had an interesting conversation with an appointment setter living in Seattle, who works for a roofing company in Chehalis (Lewis County).

The Seattle guy lives in Capitol Hill neighborhood and tells me that Chaz/Chopp Summer of Love was "necessary." He told me that public schools in Washington State are "great." 

I just let him ramble on.

I was a little taken aback that he called me at 8:03am on a Sunday morning. 

But what struck me most was how he viewed Washington State as being in good shape, which is the farthest thing from reality.

For the icing on our conversation, I asked him what he thought of Seattle City Mayor Katie Wilson. 

And his response was, "She's doing the best she can. She just needs more time to get acclimated to her new job."

So, Edgar, the roofing salesman is coming to my house tomorrow at 11:00am.  We'll see how it goes. 

Frankly, we really can't afford to replace our 24+ year old roof because of the taxes we must pay to state and county government. 

There aren't any HUD financing programs for home repairs for the middle class. HUD only offers such programs if you're below poverty level.

The roof isn't leaking yet, but it's getting old.

If only we could keep more of our state and county tax dollars, then I would have enough money to replace my roof, paint the exterior of my house, replace the broken toilet, and replace the vinyl flooring that's cracking and peeling away.

I guess these are pie in the sky dreams on my part because I'm being TAXED TO DEATH in Washington State, and I can't afford to replace our broken toilet.

QUIRKY COLLEGE DEGREES

See quirky majors offered by Washington colleges — and how much graduates make

August 30, 2026

Choosing a major can be a difficult process for college students.

Sometimes, students have to choose between their personal interests and a field that might provide more career opportunities and financial stability.

Fortunately, colleges and universities across the United States offer a number of "weird but cool" fields of study that "prove your passion can become your profession," according to scholarship search platform Fastweb.

What are some of the most unique majors offered at Washington colleges? How much do graduates earn?

McClatchy Media looked through lists at Fastweb, Yahoo Finance and Prepscholar to find quirky and unique fields of study.

Here are some of the most unusual majors available in the Evergreen State — and how much graduates earn:

Which quirky college majors are offered at colleges in Washington State?

Looking for your dream major?
 
Colleges across Washington State offer study programs that veer off the beaten path.

"If you have a passion, whether it's bagpiping, beekeeping or building wooden boats, chances are there's a degree program designed around it," Fastweb said. "These unconventional majors prove that your interests — no matter how niche — can lead to fulfilling professions."

Viticulture and enology, Washington State University

Are you a wine lover? Washington State University in Richland offers an undergraduate degree in winemaking through its Viticulture and Enology program.

The program blends "science, creativity, and business to prepare students for leadership in the wine industry," the Viticulture and Enology website says. "Through hands-on experience in grape cultivation and winemaking, and active engagement in industry-driven research, students help shape a more innovative and sustainable future for wine.

According to online employment marketplace ZipRecruiter, winemakers earn $73,832 a year on average in Washington State.

Canadian studies, University of Washington in Seattle

Want to learn more about our neighbors to the north? You can get an undergraduate degree in Canadian studies at the University of Washington in Seattle. You can even minor in Arctic studies.

Inspired by an "expanding web" of cross-border connections, the Center for Canadian Studies said it has developed "strong specializations in trade, security, Arctic foreign policy, Aboriginal self-determination and environmental management."

You can get a similar degree at Western Washington University in Bellingham.

ZipRecruiter says you can make an average of $90,425 a year with an international studies degree.

Astrobiology, University of Washington

If you love looking up at the stars, a degree in astrobiology may be the right choice for you.

Astrobiology, the study of life in the universe, is offered as an undergraduate and master's program at the University of Washington.

Students in this "diverse and vibrant" program participate in research aimed at "understanding Earth's past environments and life, exploring life in extreme environments today and studying the possibilities for life on within our solar system and on extra-solar planets," the UW astrobiology program said its website.

According to ZipRecruiter, you can earn an average of $58,827 a year in Washington State with an astrobiology degree.

Human-centered technology design, University of Washington
The University of Washington's Human-Centered Technology Design program encourages undergraduate and graduate students to design solutions for human needs, interests and global challenges.

"We advance systems and technologies for people and communities to create accessible, sustainable and prosperous futures," the Human-Centered Technology Design website says.

text:
Chicago mass shooting leaves 1 dead, 13 others injured on South Side, CPD says

A mass shooting on Chicago’s South Side late Saturday night left one man dead and 13 other people injured.

What we know:
Officers were in the 5400 block of S. Cottage Grove around 11:37 p.m. to disperse a large crowd when the shooting happened, according to the Chicago Police Department.

Unknown gunmen began firing into the crowd and hit several victims:

A 35-year-old man was shot multiple times. He was taken to the University of Chicago Medical Center, where he died.
A 34-year-old man was shot in the right shoulder. He was also taken to U of C and was listed in good condition.
A 39-year-old man was shot in the right leg and arm. He was taken to Stroger Hospital in good condition.
A 40-year-old woman was shot in the right shoulder and taken to Stroger Hospital in good condition.
A 45-year-old woman was shot in the left leg. She self-transported to St. Bernard Hospital and was listed in good condition.
A 26-year-old woman was shot multiple times in her chest. She was taken to U of C in good condition.
A 42-year-old man was shot in the leg and was taken to U of C in good condition.
A 37-year-old woman was also shot. The hospital she was taken to and her condition were not known as of 5 a.m.
A 23-year-old man was also shot. Where he was taken and his condition were also not known as of 5 a.m.
A 35-year-old man was also shot. His condition and where he was taken were also unclear.

Later on Sunday morning, Chicago police said they found four more victims:

A 47-year-old woman who was taken to Northwestern Memorial Hospital in serious condition.
A 23-year-old woman was taken to U of C in fair condition.
A 43-year-old woman was taken to U of C in fair condition.
A 21-year-old woman was taken to U of C in fair condition.

What we don't know:
It was unclear why the large gathering took place.

Police provided no description of the shooters.

Area detectives are investigating.

Reward offer
What you can do:
The Cook County Crime Stoppers is offering a cash reward of up to $10,000 for information leading to the arrest of the gunman.

"This senseless act of violence has devastated another Chicago community and left families dealing with unimaginable pain. One person lost their life, nine others were injured, and the individuals responsible must be held accountable," said Paul Rutherford, executive director of Cook County Crime Stoppers, in a statement. "We are asking everyone in the community to do the right thing. If you know who was responsible, if you heard something, saw something, or have information that could help detectives, please come forward. You can remain completely anonymous. You don't have to put yourself or your family at risk. Let Crime Stoppers be the middleman and help law enforcement get the information they need to solve this case."

text:
Lonzo Ball reveals how the China incident changed his brothers' entire basketball careers

"All because of that China shit, bro"

"I’m playing with the Lakers. They interviewing me... 'your brother’s in China, incarcerated. What do you have to say about that?' I’m like, huh?"

"they didn't even get him there. They got him at the hotel... it was just on lockdown. And then ended up having to come back home"

"they told him he was like suspended indefinitely. So then that’s when my dad was like, 'fuck does that mean? We supposed to just sit here and like wait?'"

"once that happened, that’s when he pivoted and that’s how they started hooping overseas. That's how the JBA started"

"Without the China shit, G stays in college... he probably would have to stay until Melo came and then that probably would have been his way to get in. Boom. Both of them. That's how another timeline probably went"

text:
Stonewall Jackson Statue (10/30/1875)

Sir,—As treasurer of the committee which carried out the statue of Stonewall Jackson lately presented to the State of Virginia, I must offer some remarks upon your leading article on the subject in The Times of to-day. That article offers very good reasons why, in presence of the heroic deeds and pathetic death of that remarkable man, Englishmen should have been stirred to offer a tribute of sympathy for his loss to his native State at a time when their feelings had been so powerfully moved, as by other appeals, so especially by the brilliant letters of your Correspondent from the Army of Virginia. You conclude, however, by laying down that “it is peculiarly unfortunate, then, that Englishmen should have gone out of their way to revive half-buried resentments by glorifying the prowess of a Confederate soldier, and by calling forth a display of Southern hatred of the North in the chief town of the Confederacy.” 

My answer to this (only premising that I cannot trace the “hatred of the North,” unless it is to be constructively inferred from the liberal display of the British colours which you note) is simply that the money for the statue was collected and the commission intrusted to Mr. Foley within a few weeks after the news of Jackson’s death had reached England. The subsequent delay is due to the ill-health, and, lately, the death of Foley, the competition of his many other engagements, and his anxiety to perfect the likeness. No doubt the South was “down on its luck” in what now appears by retrospect a very short time after the means had been collected for the statue; and then its promoters had two courses open to them. Either they might court the favour of the more powerful and successful side by disappointing the defeated and unhappy community whom they had led to expect the gift, or they might keep their word, although those to whom they had pledged it were unfortunate. I cannot conceive gentlemen hesitating for the infinitesimal fragment of a second over the choice. We carried on the work to which we had pledged ourselves, and for which we had sufficient means intrusted to our honour by contributors (some anonymous) who desired to see that accomplished; but we did it so quietly that the memory of it had completely faded out of the public mind until it was revived by the contribution of Foley’s posthumous statue to last season’s Exhibition of the Royal Academy, when, if ever, the protest against it should have been made. On the completion of the work it was tendered to Virginia in the unostentatious way of a letter posted to the Governor of the State, to be used at his discretion. That the Governor—the choice of a constituency in which universal suffrage now implies no distinction between white and black—should have on his own motion laid that letter before the Legislature of Virginia then in Session; that the Legislature—equally the emanation of bi-colour votes—should have eagerly voted a large supply to do honour to the gift; that a site should have been granted for it before the State Capitol, and that the ceremony of its unveiling should have been accompanied by circumstances for my first knowledge of which I am indebted to your telegram, only prove that the gift was appreciated by grateful recipients. They have no relevancy as to the duty of those in England—of those who held the money to make the statue; these would, of course, have been much disappointed at an unfriendly reception of their communication; but they are as little responsible for what has just taken place in Virginia as they were capable of foreseeing such a turn of events ten years ago when Richmond fell before the army of Grant. Had the tender of the statue been distasteful or inconvenient to the Executive, the Legislature, and the people of Virginia, it would, I make no doubt, have been refused or (if accepted) slurred over; but the donors would have discharged their responsibility. The result shows that it has much gratified a Commonwealth which speaks our language, and which still entertains such friendly feelings towards a country from which it derives its descent, that the Legislature last year made an official holyday of the Queen’s birthday. I should have thought that those who are most eager for international amity would have been the first to welcome spontaneous expressions of brotherly love between England and a Commonwealth which represents the very oldest of all our Colonies, and whose founders were Elizabeth and Raleigh. The Southern States of America, though beaten, are not annihilated, and I do not understand, either on moral or political grounds, why out of all the communities of the earth their friendship alone should not be worth our having. Whatever they may be, they are not now Slave States, and the white inhabitants of Virginia and the Carolinas are our special flesh and blood no less than those of New York and Massachusetts. Equally desirable is the friendship of the Northern States, and no voice of those who helped the Jackson statue will, I am sure, be heard against any tokens of sympathy passing between those States and England. If the admirers of Stonewall Jackson have given him a statue in Richmond, the admirers of Lincoln have given him a steeple in London, and the hottest partisans of the South have never uttered a complaint that Mr. Newman Hall’s Christchurch should be the handsomer by its “Lincoln Tower.”
Yours faithfully,
A. J. B. BERESFORD HOPE.
Arklow-house, Oct. 29.

text:
ONE MORNING YOU OWN A COMPANY YOU NEVER BOUGHT:

No ballot, no bill, no phone call. You go to bed holding shares in one business and wake up holding shares in two, and not a cent left your account to make it happen.

That event is a spinoff. The takeaway before the detail: for a stretch of weeks afterwards, the newly separated company gets sold hard by people who never formed an opinion about it, and some of them do not get a choice. Working out who those sellers are, and who wrote the terms they are selling into, is most of what the words "special situations" actually mean.

WHAT IS ACTUALLY HAPPENING

A company decides one of its divisions should be its own listed business. Instead of selling it to somebody else, the board hands it to the people who already own the parent.

The steps are fixed and published in advance. The board sets a distribution ratio - say one share of the new company for every four parent shares held. It names a record date, which decides who qualifies, and a distribution date, when the shares actually appear. Between those two dates the new company often trades on a when-issued basis, meaning it can be bought and sold before it exists in anybody's account.

Then the shares turn up. Nobody bought anything. Nobody was asked.

THE ARITHMETIC, IN ROUND INVENTED NUMBERS

Nothing below is a real company.

You hold 100 shares of a parent at $60, so $6,000. The ratio is one for four, so 25 shares of the new company land in the account. Say they open at $12 - $300 in total. The parent, now missing that division, should open near $57, or $5,700.

$5,700 plus $300 is $6,000. The morning created nothing. One holding became two.

WHAT YOU PAID GETS SPLIT TOO

Cost basis is simply what you paid, the figure a gain or loss is measured from. It does not survive the morning intact, and the rules here are kinder than most people expect.

Under Section 355 of the US tax code, a qualifying spinoff is tax-free when it happens. No gain, no loss, nothing owed for receiving shares you did not buy. Instead your original cost is divided between the two holdings in proportion to what each is worth immediately afterwards.

Keep the example running. Suppose you paid $40 a share, so $4,000 of basis. The parent is 95% of the value and the new company 5%, so $3,800 stays with the parent at $38 a share and $200 moves across at $8 a share.

Those percentages are not something to guess at. The company publishes them, on an IRS form numbered 8937 and titled Report of Organizational Actions Affecting Basis of Securities, normally posted on its own investor page.

Two more lines worth carrying. Your holding period comes with you: if you had owned the parent three years, the new shares count as three years old on day one, which matters because a stock sold within a year of purchase is taxed at the higher short-term rate. And ratios rarely divide evenly - if your holding entitled you to 25.4 shares, the broker sells the fraction and sends cash. That small cash payment is taxable, and it is the only part of the whole event that is.

WHO SELLS, AND WHY IT IS NOT ABOUT THE BUSINESS

Here is the mechanism that creates the situation, and it is close to invisible from outside.

An index fund has one job: hold the companies in an index, in the right proportions, and nothing else. S&P Dow Jones Indices, the firm that decides which companies belong in the best-known US stock indexes, standardized how it handles these separations in September 2015. For any spinoff dated on or after October 1, 2015, the new company is added to the index temporarily at a price of zero, and then, if it does not meet that index's own size and eligibility rules, it is removed on its first ordinary day of trading, at that day's closing price.

Read it again with a fund manager's job in mind. Funds tracking that index receive shares nobody there chose, and then have to sell them on a known day, at whatever the market offers that afternoon, because holding something the index no longer contains is the one thing the fund is not allowed to do.

Other sellers queue up behind, for reasons equally unrelated to the business:

- A fund whose rules say it owns large companies cannot keep a small one, and the separated division is usually the smaller half.
- Someone who held the parent for its dividend now owns a slice of something that may pay nothing at all.
- The new position is tiny. In the example above it is 5% of what was held - too small for a large investor to spend an afternoon on, and easy to sweep out.
- Almost nobody publishes research on it yet. The analysts covering the parent start the new company with little or no coverage at all.

For a while, then, the price is being set by people whose reason for selling has nothing to do with what the company earns.

THE HALF NOBODY EXPLAINS: THE PARENT WROTE THE TERMS

This is where the appeal of that last section has to be checked, hard.

The parent decides what leaves with the child. Which borrowings go along. Which contracts follow. What the new company pays the parent for shared services during the handover, and for how long. In some separations the departing business borrows money and pays the parent a large cash dividend on its way out, which means it starts its independent life already owing that money to a lender.

So the identical event can be a good business being freed from a big slow one, or a slow business being handed to shareholders wearing all the debt the parent preferred not to carry. On the morning the shares appear, those two look exactly the same.

WHY THE RANKING COLUMN IS WRONG FOR A YEAR

Stock screens sort companies by figures like the price-to-earnings ratio - the share price divided by the profit attached to one share. For a newly separated company, both halves of that fraction are unreliable for a while.

The history it publishes is carve-out accounting: what the division would have earned, with a slice of the parent's head-office costs assigned to it. Standing alone it now needs its own finance staff, its own auditors, its own listing costs, its own insurance, and those usually run higher than the slice it was allocated. So the profit figure in that ratio belongs to a company that no longer exists.

The parent's numbers break in the opposite direction. Its earnings from last year include a business it no longer owns, so comparing this year to last across the separation date compares two different companies wearing the same name.

Neither is anybody's error. The column simply has nothing sensible to put there yet.

WHERE THE ANSWERS ARE PUBLISHED

All of it is written down, in one place, before a single share arrives. A company being separated this way registers with the Securities and Exchange Commission on a document called a Form 10, and attaches an information statement, which is effectively the new company's own introduction to the public: what it does, who runs it, what it earns, what it owes. It is free, and it sits on the regulator's public site and usually the company's investor page.

Four things worth hunting for in it:

- The stated reason for the separation, in the company's own words.
- Exactly how much debt the new company leaves with, and whether it is paying anything to the parent on the way out.
- The estimate of what running independently will cost - the number the carve-out history above does not contain.
- Whether it intends to pay a dividend, and what the parent intends to do with its own.

WHAT THIS DOES NOT SETTLE

Spinoffs are not automatically cheap, and the reasoning here stops well short of saying so. A seller with no choice can produce a price disconnected from the business, which is a reason the price might be wrong - not evidence that the business is any good. Those are two different claims and only the first one follows.

The first two or three quarters are also the messiest a newly independent company will ever report, thick with one-off separation costs and a cost base still settling down. A rough opening report is not proof of much either.

And it cuts both ways. Sometimes the parent keeps the better half and knows it.

WHERE THIS QUESTION LIVES

The Deep-Value and Special-Situations Len5 hunts a business priced under what it looks worth, or one carrying a dated event that has not played out, and a spinoff is the second of those in its purest form - it arrives with real dates attached: a record date, a distribution date, and a day the index funds have to be finished. What settles the case is whether any discount is still there once those compulsory sellers are done and the company has reported two clean quarters showing its actual standalone costs. If the gap closes the same week the index selling ends, there was never anything underneath it.

The Quality-Value Len5 wants a durable business at a fair price, and a separation is one of the rare moments a business gets priced on its own for the first time in its life. Durability is the half to test rather than assume here: whether the new company can win customers without the parent's name on the door, and whether it still leans on the parent for services once the handover agreements run out. Two or three years of stable margins under its own roof is what would answer it.

The Income Len5 watches cash genuinely reaching owners and genuinely funded by the business, and a spinoff quietly rearranges exactly that. A parent that has just become smaller frequently resets its own dividend, and the two payments afterwards can add up to less than the single payment before. The test is identical on both sides of the split: whether the payment sits comfortably inside the cash that business generates now, rather than inside what the combined company used to produce.

A merger needs a vote. A purchase needs a decision. A spinoff needs nothing from you at all, which makes it the only way a stock lands in an ordinary account without anyone choosing it, and the only one where the homework starts after you already own the thing.

Not investment advice.

text:
Ohio Principal Loses His Job After Taking In a Homeless Student — And Says He Has No Regrets.

Rob Burnside spent 31 years in education as principal of Lakota East High School near Cincinnati.

When a student named Landerius “DeDe” Hayes became homeless and was told he had to withdraw after his mother moved outside the district, Burnside and his wife took the teenager into their home.

District officials said they no longer believed he could be an effective leader. He was given the choice to step down or face termination. He left.

Hayes later offered to move back so Burnside wouldn’t lose his job. Burnside told him: “No. You’re gonna stay with me… You’re part of this family.”

They became his legal guardians. Hayes graduated this past May. Burnside still can’t get a principal job in the area. He has no regrets.

text:
"I disagree on your relevancy determinations and with regard to social media specifically, anonymous criticism of government is not really valid. This is my opinion but I’m open to changing it if you have contradicting evidence."

I mean... I can't challenge that with "evidence" because it's an opinion. An extremely wrong one that is not supported even remotely by constitutional interpretation, but still an opinion. Everyone is entitled to their own wrong opinions. 

But if you like, I'll offer McIntyre v. Ohio Elections Commission, where anonymous political speech is explicitly founded to be protected by the first amendment. 

"You are conflating real life privacy with online privacy. I don’t believe online privacy has achieved much success in guaranteeing anyone more freedom, and the opposite is true for child victims. Thanks to the anonymous internet, children have had less freedom."

No, I'm explicitly trying to reject forcibly conflating those two things, which is what mandating some sort of digital real ID and stripping pseudonymity from people would do.  

As for the rest, I reiterate what I said to the OP: I legitimately do not [care about other people's families outside my social group], no. No more than you legitimately care about mine. I tire of people treating parasocial empathy as legitimate concern. Parasocial empathy is just a hostage puppy, and I reject hostage puppies as a valid reason to surrender basic freedoms or give the government expanded control. 

I do not want a paternalistic government. Governments are always bad parents.

text: Vivek still hasn't adjusted his plan to deal with the real issue. People don't want to be forced to have a data center in their community. Right now, big tech lawyers are threatening Ohio communities with bankrupting lawsuits if they don't get approval for their mega data center. That is force pure and simple. Human nature rejects anything being forced on us, regardless of how wonderful we are told it is. Nothing in Vivek's plan addresses that force. He merely offers freebies to you and makes arguments that sound like he'll make you happy to be the object of force. That just does not fly. His plan will not convince voters until he includes the one thing that removes the force, and that is a vote for local citizens on a data center locating in their area. With that, knowing they have the final say, people can remain calm enough to listen to the sales pitch and then take it or leave it. Let people know that it's fine if they don't want a data center because there are plenty of other communities that may welcome one. Cater to that other aspect of human nature that makes people tend to want something they think they can't have. Working with human nature and not against it will result in both more data centers and more happy voters. Until an approach like this is implemented the data center opposition will not go away, it will only get louder. Vivek could cruise into the Governorship and become a national leader on the data center issue if he embraces such a plan.

text:
Tomorrow is Tim Cook's last day as the CEO of Apple.

 In 2009, when Steve Jobs was suffering from liver failure, Cook discovered they shared a rare blood type. After undergoing invasive tests at a remote clinic to confirm compatibility, Cook offered to donate a portion of his own liver. Jobs flatly and furiously rejected the offer, shouting from his bed, "I'll never let you do that!"

Before joining Apple in 1998, Cook worked 12 years at IBM and had just accepted a vice president role at Compaq (then the world's largest PC manufacturer). Every financial advisor and mentor told him leaving a booming Compaq for a near-bankrupt Apple was career suicide, but he famously decided to join within five minutes of meeting Jobs.

Growing up the son of a shipyard worker and pharmacy employee in small-town Alabama, Cook started delivering newspapers before dawn as a young teenager and later worked at an aluminum plant during college summers.

Unlike many Silicon Valley CEOs with software or design backgrounds, Cook graduated with an industrial engineering degree from Auburn. His obsession with eliminating friction and waste stems from factory floor optimization models.

text:
I didn't write this but I do feel it's relevant. And I have the same misgivings about Trump, esp about this whole Iran thing... 

I have to admit, I’m enjoying watching some of my friends suddenly discover their deep, almost sacred reverence for historic names now that Donald Trump has renamed Lake Ontario “Lake America.”

Where was this passionate defense of tradition when we spent the last decade playing cultural Mad Libs with names?

The Cleveland Indians became the Guardians.
The Washington Redskins became the Commanders.
Aunt Jemima was evicted from the breakfast table and replaced by Pearl Milling Company.
Uncle Ben got demoted to Ben’s Original.
The Native American woman disappeared from Land O’Lakes butter.
Eskimo Pie became Edy’s Pie.
The Dixie Chicks became The Chicks.
Lady Antebellum became Lady A.
Universities and real-estate professionals started replacing “master bedroom” with “primary bedroom.”
Computer programmers began retiring “master/slave” terminology.
Schools, streets, statues and buildings bearing the names of historical figures were renamed by the hundreds.
Then there were the military bases.
Fort Bragg became Fort Liberty.
Fort Hood became Fort Cavazos.
Fort Benning became Fort Moore.
Fort Polk became Fort Johnson.
Fort Lee became Fort Gregg-Adams.
Fort Gordon became Fort Eisenhower.
Fort Rucker became Fort Novosel.
Fort Pickett became Fort Barfoot.
Fort A.P. Hill became Fort Walker.
We even watched Mount McKinley become Denali.

Meanwhile, our vocabulary got its own remodeling job. “Mothers” sometimes became birthing people, “pregnant women” became pregnant people, and “breastfeeding” acquired the alternative chestfeeding in some institutional language.

And Columbus Day? Plenty of cities, states and institutions decided Indigenous Peoples’ Day was preferable.

For years the message was: Names matter. Words matter. Language evolves. Old names can be changed when society decides another name better reflects its values. If you're offended by the change, get over it.

Okay.

Apparently there was an asterisk:

This principle remains valid until Donald Trump names something.

Suddenly the people who spent a decade redecorating the dictionary have chained themselves to the furniture.

Personally, I think Lake America is mostly political theater, and pretty funny political theater at that. Canada is perfectly free to keep calling it Lake Ontario. Nobody is confiscating their maps.

But after watching everything from pancake syrup to Army installations get renamed in the name of cultural sensitivity, I simply cannot work up the appropriate level of outrage over a lake.

So to my friends who are losing sleep over Lake America, I offer the same compassionate advice we Conservatives received during the Great Renaming:

Language changes. Names evolve. Try to keep up.

text:
WBC Heavyweight Champion Tim Witherspoon eats a left hand from challenger Pinklon Thomas, on August 31, 1984, at the Riviera Hotel & Casino in Las Vegas.

Thomas wins a 12-round majority decision, in Witherspoon's first title defense, to join Larry Homes (IBF) and Gerrie Coetzee (WBA) as an alphabet titlist.

For Pinklon Thomas, all kidding aside, it's a monumental win. Not just in the ring but in life.

From Sports Illustrated's report on this bout (Excerpts, not the full article):

A child of the meanest streets of Pontiac, Michigan, Thomas had a $150 a day heroin habit by the time he was 14.
"When you have habits," he said then, "you have ways of getting the money. I won't say how, but most of the guys I ran with are either dead or in prison."
His life was a nightmare of drugs, pills, alcohol and street fights.
"I was always the youngest, but I was as big or bigger than anybody else," Thomas said this night with a sad smile. "People were pushing me to see if I'd fight.
When I was 15 a big 34-year-old guy named Geronimo rapped me with a cue stick in a pool hall. He was high on downers. I took him out and hit him nine times and put him in a hospital."
He was 17 when he married Kathy Jones. "She's a gift," he said then. A few months later, Kathy enlisted in the Army. Pinklon joined her at Fort Jackson in South Carolina. Then they moved to Fort Lewis, Wash., near Seattle. Thomas had put his habit aside—cold turkey—at Fort Jackson, but it followed him and Kathy on the 3,000-mile bus trip to Fort Lewis, and took over his life again.
Thomas added: "Then one day a friend sent me to a gym to see a trainer named Joe West. I used to tell people I had 15 fights back in Detroit. Then West used me for meat. He put me in the ring with a guy named Big Ben. I was high on heroin and speed. For two rounds I outjabbed him. Then I got tired, and he almost killed me."
Thomas, who was by then 19, wanted revenge.
He began to run in the morning. "I'd run and I'd throw up. Then I'd run some more and I'd throw up some more. I stopped the drugs. Six months later I ran that Big Ben out of the gym."
After three amateur fights, Thomas turned pro.
He was 15-0 when he, Kathy and Pinklon Thomas III moved to Philadelphia in 1981.
His biggest fight came in January 1983 when he held Coetzee to a draw.
"I thought I'd won," he said then. "But I wasn't bitter. I thought, 'If I can beat a guy like that, the No. 1 contender, I can beat anybody.' They told me not to stand in front of him, that he'd kill me with that big right hand. I don't like people to tell me things like that. I stood in front of him and he never hit me."
Thomas won four more fights and was ranked #3 when Don King offered him the fight against Witherspoon.
"Saturday is young Pink's eighth birthday," Thomas said the afternoon before the bout. "I asked him what he wanted. He asked me for the championship belt. I'm going to give it to him."
Thomas is a flat-footed, stand-up boxer with good reflexes and a jab that could batter down doors. "It's as close to a Sonny Liston jab as I've ever seen," said trainer Angelo Dundee, who trained Liston's conqueror, Ali, and who was brought in to work with Thomas for the  Witherspoon fight. "It's a hard jab, and he's going to win the title with it."
That proved one of Dundee's better predictions.
After one round of testing, Thomas, who came in at 216 pounds, drilled the jab into Witherspoon's face and left it there for the next eight rounds; by the second round, the 217-pound Witherspoon was blinking furiously.
"He's thumbing me," the champion complained to referee Richard Steele, who saw no wrongdoing. Three rounds later, Steele took a point away from Witherspoon for backhanding.
After building an overwhelming lead, Thomas coasted through the last three rounds.
The scoring should have been academic. It wasn't.
One judge, Hal Miller, who must have arrived around the 11th round, or been on the take, scored it even. The other two, Dalby Shirley (115-112) and Duane Ford (116-112), both had it for Thomas.
Half an hour after the decision, Thomas, holding an ice bag to his left eye, slumped in a chair in his large and silent dressing room. Nearby, Kathy, dressed in pink, talked quietly with a friend. Across the room young Pinklon leaned against a wall, the WBC belt draped across one small shoulder. Lifting his head, the new champion studied his son. Then, with a small grin, he raised a fist and said, very softly, "Can you believe it? The championship belt."

Thomas entered rehab, after binging on drugs and alcohol for five days, in 1989.

"I’ve been 100% clean since February 10, 1989," Thomas said in 2013.

Thomas now has a foundation, Project P.I.N.K. (Pride in Neighborhood Kids), and is a motivational speaker.

text:
Jensen Huang listed five things AI is doing to America. I went through them against the public record. Four hold up. Two need a footnote, and the more interesting one is about timing rather than accuracy.

Manufacturing coming back. This one has concrete under it. SK hynix broke ground on a $4bn advanced packaging plant in Indiana on Thursday. Micron is building in New York and Idaho and expanding in Japan. Intel's $7bn packaging plant in Malaysia opens in the second half of this year. Coherent is expanding InP capacity in Texas. These are real sites with real permits.

Demand driving investment in the grid. Also true, and this week it got quantified from the other direction.

Construction and manufacturing jobs. Follows from the first, and shows up in the county-level filings around each of those sites.

$400bn into AI startups in six months. Verified, and slightly understated. PitchBook has $407bn for the first half of 2026, against $264bn for all of 2025. AI took roughly 86% of every US venture dollar in that window.

Here is footnote one. Of that $407bn, about $217bn went to OpenAI and Anthropic. More than half of the number, to two companies that already existed. The figure was offered as evidence that AI is creating new companies and industries, and it is better evidence that capital is concentrating into two of them.

Footnote two is the phrase "powered by market forces, not subsidies." The market forces are doing most of the work, and the subsidies are also there. Coherent disclosed a $50m preliminary memorandum under the CHIPS Act to support its Sherman expansion. In July the Commerce Department announced letters of intent worth $874m across seven companies, with up to $300m of that going to GlobalFoundries specifically to accelerate co-packaged optics by two to three years. Both things are true at once.

Now the part I find most useful, because two CEOs described opposite ends of the same gap within three days of each other.

Huang: AI is creating demand that drives investment in our aging power grid.

Musk, on Saturday: roughly 15GW of AI compute produced in 2027 cannot be turned on in 2027, because you also need the transformers, the wiring, the liquid cooling, the chillers and the networking. He added that this is harder than just finding the power.

Both are correct. Huang is describing the demand signal, which is arriving now. Musk is describing the delivery, which is not.

Line up the dates and the gap is visible. The capital lands in 2026: $407bn into startups, $279bn of NVIDIA supply commitments, groundbreakings in Indiana and Malaysia. The capacity lands later: Micron's converted Taiwan fab in 2027, Samsung's P5 Fab 1 in 2028, SK hynix's Indiana cleanroom in October 2028, HBM4E volume in 2029, Micron New York in 2030.

Between the money and the machines there is a two-year hole, and 15GW is what somebody put in it.

That does not make the reindustrialisation thesis wrong. It makes it slower than the capital commitment implies, and it locates the binding constraint somewhere unglamorous. Not chips. Not power generation. Transformers, switchgear, cable and cooling, delivered and installed on a schedule.

What I would watch: whether any of these operators starts reporting energised capacity separately from contracted capacity. Right now the announcements are denominated in dollars and the constraint is denominated in delivery slots, and those two units do not convert.

text:
EXCLUSIVE:  Laura Loomer 

🚨 Angie Nixon’s Jacksonville communist themed café listed as *delinquent* on state food license, further revealing her disregard for Florida Laws 🚨 

Cafe Resistance Bookstore & Coffee Shop, the Jacksonville business owned by Democrat U.S. Senate nominee Angie Nixon @AngieNixon, appears in Florida Department of Business and Professional Regulation (DBPR) records dated Aug. 20, 2026, as a permanent food-service operation with a license status of “Delinquent” and “Active.”

The license expiration date is listed as June 1, 2026. By late August, the shop had been past due for roughly 11 weeks.
In Florida, a food-service establishment that continues operating after its license expires is treated as unlicensed. 

“Delinquent, Active” is the state’s designation for a license that has not been renewed but has not been formally closed. Cafe Resistance, opened in 2024, functions as more than a coffee shop. It sells books, including titles restricted in some Florida schools for sexualizing children; operates a community pantry that has offered free Plan B and other supplies; and has been used for voter registration and neighborhood events. 

Nixon has described the business as a community hub and a response to state book restrictions. The DBPR filing does not, by itself, show whether the shop has stopped serving food or whether a renewal is pending. It does show that the required food-service license has lapsed for nearly three months while the business remained listed as active.

Nixon won the Democrat Senate primary this month and will face Republican Sen. Ashley Moody @SenAshleyMoody in November. 

As @LoomeredStrat Loomered Strategies has previously exposed, Angie Nixon has multiple serious traffic citations, she has had multiple accidents, and she drove into oncoming traffic with her daughter in the car, injuring a minor and causing thousands of dollars of damage. Angie then stiffed the hospital for the medical bills for her daughter and herself, which resulted in a lien. 

The compliance gap at a food-service business owned by a Democrat candidate now seeking one of the state’s two U.S. Senate seats is further evidence Angie Nixon thinks she’s above the law, and thus she is unfit to hold office. ​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​
